questions.title: Fascicular arrangement of rectus femoris
questions.subject: msk
questions.module_subject: SCU-FBS102 > Anatomy > Basis of Anatomy > Muscular System
questions.source_citation: Formative and Past Exams 2021 Q39 (also 2022 Q19)
questions.question: How is the rectus femoris muscle architecturally classified based on its fascicular arrangement?

options.D: The massive highly branched multipennate design

explanations.A: Incorrect. A unipennate muscle, such as flexor pollicis longus, has its fascicles running obliquely into only one side of a central tendon. Rectus femoris has fascicles converging onto its tendon from both sides, which is the bipennate pattern, not unipennate.
explanations.B: Correct. Rectus femoris is bipennate: its fibres run obliquely to a central tendon that lies in the middle of the muscle, with fascicles approaching that tendon from both sides like the barbs of a feather. This arrangement packs a large number of short fibres into the muscle's cross-section, which trades range of movement for the greater force needed at the hip and knee that rectus femoris crosses. The classic textbook contrast is with sartorius, a long strap muscle built for range rather than force.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Circumpennate (or multipennate with fibres converging from all sides onto a central tendon, as in deltoid) is not how rectus femoris is described; the muscle has one central tendon with fascicles from two sides, which is the simpler bipennate pattern.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A multipennate muscle, like deltoid, has several tendinous septa with fascicles converging on each from multiple directions. Rectus femoris has a single central tendon, so it is described as bipennate rather than multipennate.

questions.subtopic: Classification of skeletal muscle by fascicular architecture
questions.learning_objective: Classify rectus femoris as a bipennate muscle and place it correctly among the pennate muscle forms.

questions.title: Plane dividing the body into anterior and posterior parts
questions.subject: msk
questions.module_subject: SCU-FBS102 > Anatomy > Basis of Anatomy > Anatomical Terminology
questions.source_citation: Formative and Past Exams 2021 Q64 (also 2022 Q44)
questions.question: Which precise anatomical plane is mathematically used to divide the body into front anterior and back posterior portions?

options.A: The exactly completely centered median separating sagittal vertical plane
options.B: The completely horizontal dividing flat transverse level horizontal plane
options.D: The highly specialized precise completely targeted surgical cross sectional plane

explanations.A: Incorrect. The median (sagittal) plane is also vertical, but it runs in the body's midline and divides it into equal right and left halves, not into front and back. Confusing the median plane with the coronal plane is a common trap because both are vertical planes.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The horizontal (transverse) plane runs at right angles to the long axis of the body, dividing it into a superior (upper) and an inferior (lower) part rather than an anterior and a posterior part.
explanations.C: Correct. The coronal (frontal) plane is a vertical plane that runs at right angles to the median plane, cutting the body into an anterior part towards the front and a posterior part towards the back. It is one of the three standard anatomical planes, alongside the median/sagittal plane and the horizontal/transverse plane, each defined by which pair of parts it leaves behind.
explanations.D: Incorrect. There is no separate 'surgical cross-sectional plane' among the standard anatomical planes; imaging cross-sections are usually taken along the transverse plane, and this option does not name any of the three recognised anatomical planes.

questions.learning_objective: Name the coronal plane as the vertical plane dividing the body into anterior and posterior parts, distinct from the median and horizontal planes.

questions.title: Short bone of the foot shaped like a cube
questions.subject: msk
questions.source_citation: Formative and Past Exams 2021 Q48 (also 2022 Q28)
questions.question: Which of the following bones is anatomically classified as a short bone due to its cubical shape?

options.A: The flat protective posterior occipital cranial bone
options.B: The highly complex irregular temporal skull bone
options.D: The extremely long and slender fibula bone

explanations.A: Incorrect. The occipital bone is one of the flat bones of the skull, built as two thin plates of compact bone around a spongy diploe, and it protects the posterior cranial fossa rather than fitting the short-bone class.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The temporal bone is classed as an irregular bone because of its complex shape, not as a short bone; irregular bones share the internal spongy structure of short bones but do not have their compact, roughly cube-like external shape.
explanations.C: Correct. Short bones are roughly cuboidal, with a thin shell of compact bone surrounding a spongy interior, and the carpal bones of the wrist and the tarsal bones of the foot are the standard examples. The cuboid is one of the tarsal bones on the lateral side of the foot, and it is named for exactly this cube-like shape, making it the textbook example of a short bone in the foot.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The fibula is a long bone: it has an elongated shaft with two expanded ends, the opposite shape from the compact, cube-like proportions that define a short bone.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the cuboid as a tarsal bone belonging to the short-bone class because of its cubical shape.

questions.title: Classic example of a hinge joint
questions.subject: msk
questions.source_citation: EOY 2026 Q9
questions.question: Which of the following articulations is a typical example of a hinge joint?

explanations.A: Correct. The elbow is a synovial hinge joint between the humerus, ulna and radius, held by collateral ligaments that restrict it to a single axis of movement. Like other hinge joints, it is uniaxial and permits flexion and extension only, never abduction, adduction or rotation, which is exactly the property that makes it the textbook example of the class.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The shoulder is a ball-and-socket (spheroidal) synovial joint, which is multiaxial and allows flexion, extension, abduction, adduction, rotation and circumduction — the opposite of a hinge joint's single-axis restriction.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The hip is also a ball-and-socket joint, deeper and more stable than the shoulder because of the acetabulum, but multiaxial in the same way, so it does not fit the hinge-joint class either.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Cranial sutures are fibrous joints (synarthroses) with essentially no movement in the adult, joined directly by fibrous tissue rather than by a synovial cavity, so they belong to a different structural class altogether from the synovial hinge joint.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the elbow as a synovial hinge joint restricted to flexion and extension.

questions.title: Nerve cell body shape in a dorsal root ganglion
questions.subject: fnd
questions.module_subject: SCU-FBS102 > Anatomy > Basis of Anatomy > Nervous Tissue
questions.source_citation: Formative and Past Exams 2021 Q38 (also 2022 Q18)
questions.question: What specific type of nerve cell body is characteristically found within a spinal dorsal root ganglion?

options.B: The very large multipolar motor cells
options.D: The extremely small simple unipolar cells

explanations.A: Incorrect. A true bipolar neuron has two separate processes leaving opposite poles of the cell body, as seen in the retina and the vestibulocochlear ganglia — a different, rarer pattern from the single stalk of a dorsal root ganglion cell.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Multipolar neurons, with many dendrites and a single axon, are the shape of motor neurons in the anterior horn of the spinal cord, not of the sensory cell bodies packed inside a dorsal root ganglion.
explanations.C: Correct. Nerve cells are classed by how many processes leave the cell body. A dorsal root ganglion cell starts embryologically as bipolar, but its two processes fuse close to the cell body into a single stalk that then splits in a T shape into a peripheral and a central branch — so only one process appears to leave the soma, which is why the cell is called pseudounipolar rather than truly unipolar.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A genuinely unipolar cell, with one process arising directly from the cell body and no fusion of two earlier processes, is essentially absent from the human nervous system; the dorsal root ganglion cell only resembles one at low magnification, which is precisely the distinction the term 'pseudounipolar' preserves.

questions.subtopic: Classification of neurons by process number
questions.learning_objective: Identify the dorsal root ganglion cell as pseudounipolar and explain how it differs from a true unipolar or bipolar neuron.

questions.title: Muscle type associated with the viscera
questions.subject: msk
questions.module_subject: SCU-FBS102 > Anatomy > Basis of Anatomy > Muscular System
questions.source_citation: EOY 2026 Q10
questions.question: Which of the following types of muscle tissue is associated with the term viscera?

explanations.A: Correct. Smooth muscle is the involuntary muscle type that lines the walls of the hollow viscera — the gut tube, the airways, blood vessels, the bladder and the uterus — where it produces the slow, sustained or rhythmic contractions needed for functions such as peristalsis and vascular tone. It lacks the visible cross-striations of skeletal and cardiac muscle, is controlled by the autonomic nervous system rather than by voluntary command, and its spindle-shaped, single-nucleated fibres are the histological hallmark that sets it apart from the other two muscle types.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Cardiac muscle is specific to the wall of the heart; it is striated and involuntary, but it is not the tissue that lines the general run of hollow viscera such as the gut and airways, which is the property this question is asking about.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Skeletal muscle is voluntary and striated, attached to bone to move the joints, and it is not the muscle type found in the walls of the viscera.
explanations.D: Incorrect. 'Striated muscle' is a structural category covering both skeletal and cardiac muscle, which show visible cross-striations under the microscope; the viscera are lined by smooth muscle, which is specifically non-striated.

questions.learning_objective: Identify smooth muscle as the involuntary, non-striated muscle type lining the hollow viscera.

questions.title: Main divisions of the autonomic nervous system
questions.subject: neuro
questions.source_citation: EOY 2026 Q12
questions.question: The autonomic nervous system is mainly composed of which of the following divisions?

explanations.A: Incorrect. 'Somatic' names the voluntary motor and sensory system that supplies skeletal muscle and skin, which is a separate system from the autonomic nervous system altogether, not one of its two divisions.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Central and peripheral describe the anatomical split of the whole nervous system (brain and spinal cord versus everything outside them), a different axis of classification from the functional division of the autonomic outflow itself.
explanations.C: Correct. The autonomic nervous system controls visceral functions — blood pressure, gut motility and secretion, bladder emptying, sweating and more — through a two-neuron efferent pathway (preganglionic then postganglionic) that is organised into two functional divisions: the sympathetic and the parasympathetic. The two typically act in a reciprocal, balancing way on the same target organs, for example speeding the heart (sympathetic) versus slowing it (parasympathetic).
explanations.D: Incorrect. 'Motor and cranial nerve branches' is not a recognised division of the autonomic system; cranial nerves carry both somatic and autonomic (parasympathetic) fibres, so this option does not describe the autonomic system's own two-part functional organisation.

questions.subtopic: Organisation of the autonomic nervous system
questions.learning_objective: Name the sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions as the two functional components of the autonomic nervous system.

questions.title: Space between a presynaptic and postsynaptic neuron
questions.subject: neuro
questions.module_subject: SCU-FBS102 > Physiology > Cell Physiology > Intercellular Communication
questions.source_citation: Formative and Past Exams 2021 Q32 (also 2022 Q12)
questions.question: What is the anatomical term for the microscopic space located exactly between a presynaptic and a postsynaptic neuron?

options.B: The completely enclosed synaptic vesicle area
options.C: The very narrow myelin sheath gap

explanations.A: Correct. Cells signal each other at a distance through neural communication, in which a neuron releases a neurotransmitter that must cross a narrow extracellular gap to reach a contiguous cell — that gap is the synaptic cleft. It is this space that the released neurotransmitter diffuses across before binding receptors on the postsynaptic membrane, which is what converts an electrical signal in the presynaptic neuron into a chemical, and then again electrical, signal in the postsynaptic one.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Synaptic vesicles are membrane-bound sacs inside the presynaptic terminal that store neurotransmitter before release; they are a structure within the presynaptic cell, not the extracellular space between the two neurons.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The gaps in a myelin sheath are the nodes of Ranvier, which allow saltatory conduction along a single axon — an unrelated structure to the space between two separate neurons at a synapse.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The postsynaptic density is a protein-dense specialisation on the inner face of the postsynaptic membrane where receptors cluster; it is part of the postsynaptic cell's membrane, not the gap between the two cells.

questions.learning_objective: Name the synaptic cleft as the extracellular gap a neurotransmitter crosses between a presynaptic and postsynaptic neuron.

questions.title: Precursor molecule of cyclic AMP
questions.subject: fnd
questions.module_subject: SCU-FBS102 > Biochemistry > Enzymes and Cell Signalling
questions.source_citation: Formative and Past Exams 2021 Q12
questions.question: During the activation of the G protein signaling pathway from which specific precursor molecule is cyclic AMP directly derived?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Guanosine triphosphate (GTP) is the nucleotide that activates the G protein itself — the Gα subunit exchanges its bound GDP for GTP — but GTP is not the molecule that adenylate cyclase converts into cyclic AMP.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Adenosine diphosphate is a lower-energy relative of ATP, but it is not the substrate of adenylate cyclase; the enzyme acts on the triphosphate form, not the diphosphate.
explanations.C: Correct. Once a hormone binds its receptor and activates the G protein, the Gα-GTP subunit stimulates the membrane enzyme adenylate cyclase, which converts ATP into cyclic AMP (cAMP) with the release of pyrophosphate. Phosphodiesterase later degrades cAMP back down, so the balance between adenylate cyclase's synthesis and phosphodiesterase's degradation sets the second messenger's intracellular level.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Guanosine diphosphate (GDP) is the inactive, GTP-bound Gα subunit's resting state before hormone binding triggers GDP-for-GTP exchange; it plays no part in the actual synthesis of cyclic AMP by adenylate cyclase.

questions.subtopic: G protein signalling — cyclic AMP synthesis
questions.learning_objective: State that adenylate cyclase synthesises cyclic AMP from ATP, not from GTP, as part of the G-protein signalling cascade.

questions.title: Essential amino acid among the four options
questions.subject: fnd
questions.module_subject: SCU-FBS102 > Biochemistry > Amino Acids and Proteins
questions.source_citation: EOM 2026 Q1
questions.question: Which of the following is classified as an essential amino acid?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Aspartate is a fully non-essential amino acid; the body synthesises it readily from oxaloacetate by transamination, and dietary intake is not required to meet normal needs at any life stage.
explanations.B: Correct. Arginine (with histidine) is classed as semi-essential, or conditionally essential: the body can synthesise it via the urea cycle, but not fast enough to meet the increased demand of rapid growth in infancy and childhood, so dietary arginine becomes necessary at those times. Exam questions that group it simply as 'essential' are drawing this same distinction — arginine cannot be treated as freely dispensable the way the other three answer options are, which is what separates it from them here.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Asparagine, like aspartate, is a non-essential amino acid the body makes from oxaloacetate-derived intermediates without needing a dietary source.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Alanine is one of the most freely non-essential amino acids, synthesised by transamination of pyruvate and central to the glucose-alanine cycle between muscle and liver; it carries no conditional requirement the way arginine does.

questions.subtopic: Classification of amino acids by dietary essentiality
questions.learning_objective: Identify arginine, with histidine, as a semi-essential amino acid required in the diet during periods of rapid growth.

questions.title: Product of the preparatory phase of glycolysis
questions.subject: fnd
questions.source_citation: Formative and Past Exams 2021 Q27 (also 2022 Q7)
questions.question: What is the primary functional product generated directly from the preparatory phase of glycolysis?

options.B: The highly active acetyl coenzyme A

explanations.A: Incorrect. Pyruvate is the end product of the whole glycolytic pathway, made in the later energy-producing phase when each triose phosphate is oxidised and dephosphorylated — it is not what the preparatory phase itself hands off.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Acetyl coenzyme A is formed afterwards, when pyruvate dehydrogenase acts on pyruvate; this reaction happens after glycolysis is complete and outside the glycolytic pathway itself, in the mitochondrial matrix.
explanations.C: Correct. In the energy-utilising (preparatory) phase, hexokinase spends one ATP to make glucose 6-phosphate, phosphohexose isomerase converts it to fructose 6-phosphate, phosphofructokinase-1 spends a second ATP to make fructose 1,6-bisphosphate, and aldolase A then cleaves that six-carbon molecule into two three-carbon trioses — glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate and dihydroxyacetone phosphate. Glyceraldehyde (as its 3-phosphate ester) is therefore the functional three-carbon product this phase generates before the energy-producing phase can begin.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Carbon dioxide is released later, during the pyruvate dehydrogenase reaction and in the citric acid cycle, not anywhere within glycolysis itself; glycolysis produces no CO2 at all.

questions.learning_objective: State that aldolase cleaves fructose 1,6-bisphosphate into two triose phosphates, including glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate, at the end of glycolysis's preparatory phase.

questions.title: End product of the preparatory phase of glycolysis
questions.subject: fnd
questions.source_citation: Formative and Past Exams 2021 Q19 (also 2023 Q19)
questions.question: What is the major end product generated at the conclusion of the preparatory phase of the glycolysis pathway?

options.B: The highly active acetyl coenzyme A
options.D: The fatigue inducing lactic acid molecule

explanations.A: Incorrect. Pyruvate is made in the second, energy-producing phase of glycolysis, when each triose phosphate made by the preparatory phase is oxidised and dephosphorylated in a series of further steps — it is downstream of the phase this question asks about.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Acetyl coenzyme A is generated only after glycolysis finishes, by the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex acting on pyruvate in the mitochondrion, so it cannot be a product of the preparatory phase.
explanations.C: Correct. The preparatory phase ends when aldolase A cleaves fructose 1,6-bisphosphate into two three-carbon trioses, glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate and dihydroxyacetone phosphate; triose phosphate isomerase then interconverts the two so that both are ultimately processed as glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate. This is the molecule that carries all the carbon and phosphate forward into the energy-producing phase of the pathway, which is why it is named as the phase's major end product.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Lactate is formed only under anaerobic conditions, by lactate dehydrogenase acting on pyruvate after glycolysis is complete, to regenerate the NAD+ that glycolysis needs to continue — it has no role at the end of the preparatory phase.

questions.learning_objective: State that glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate is the triose that carries the carbon skeleton forward into glycolysis's energy-producing phase.

questions.title: Amino acid with no chiral centre
questions.subject: fnd
questions.module_subject: SCU-FBS102 > Biochemistry > Amino Acids and Proteins
questions.source_citation: Formative and Past Exams 2021 Q5
questions.question: Which of the following amino acids is considered optically inactive because it lacks a chiral carbon center?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Valine has a branched side chain attached to its alpha carbon along with an amino group, a carboxyl group and a hydrogen — four different groups — which makes its alpha carbon chiral (asymmetric) and gives valine optical activity.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Alanine's alpha carbon carries a methyl side chain in addition to the amino group, carboxyl group and hydrogen, again four different substituents, so it too has a chiral centre and is optically active.
explanations.C: Correct. Glycine is the one amino acid whose side chain is a single hydrogen atom, so its alpha carbon is bonded to two identical hydrogen atoms along with the amino and carboxyl groups. With only three distinct groups rather than four, the alpha carbon is not asymmetric, which makes glycine the only amino acid with no chiral centre and therefore the only one that is optically inactive.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Leucine has a bulky branched side chain on its alpha carbon, giving it four different substituents and a chiral centre exactly like the other 19 standard amino acids apart from glycine.

questions.learning_objective: Identify glycine as the one amino acid with no asymmetric alpha carbon, making it optically inactive.

questions.title: Bonds stabilising protein secondary structure
questions.subject: fnd
questions.source_citation: Formative and Past Exams 2021 Q73 (also 2022 Q52)
questions.question: The structural stability of the secondary structure of a functional protein is maintained and stabilized by which bonds?

options.A: The extremely strong completely totally unbreakable covalent disulphide bonds
options.C: The highly charged tightly bound completely electrostatic ionic bonds
options.D: The highly basic entirely totally strict simple linear peptide bonds

explanations.A: Incorrect. Disulphide bonds are covalent links between the sulfhydryl groups of two cysteine residues; they help stabilise tertiary and quaternary structure by cross-linking distant parts of a folded chain, not the regular, repeating secondary-structure coils and sheets.
explanations.B: Correct. Secondary structure is the regular local folding of the polypeptide backbone into forms such as the alpha-helix or the beta-pleated sheet. The alpha-helix, for example, is held together by hydrogen bonds forming between the NH group of one peptide bond and the C=O group of another peptide bond further along the same chain, and beta-sheets are similarly held together by hydrogen bonds between backbone atoms of aligned chain segments — this hydrogen bonding of the backbone, not the side chains, is what defines and stabilises secondary structure.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Ionic (electrostatic) bonds form between oppositely charged amino acid side chains and contribute to tertiary structure, holding the folded three-dimensional shape together, rather than the local backbone coiling of secondary structure.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Peptide bonds are the covalent bonds that link amino acids into the polypeptide chain in the first place, defining primary structure; they do not by themselves fold the chain into a helix or sheet, which is what secondary structure describes.

questions.learning_objective: State that hydrogen bonds between backbone atoms hold together the alpha-helix and beta-pleated sheet of secondary structure.

questions.title: Type of inhibition from covalent enzyme blockers
questions.subject: fnd
questions.source_citation: Formative and Past Exams 2021 Q14
questions.question: Certain toxic compounds inhibit the acetylcholinesterase enzyme by forming strong bonds. What type of inhibition is this?

options.C: The reversible non competitive allosteric activation
options.D: A simple negative feedback inhibition pathway

explanations.A: Incorrect. A reversible competitive inhibitor binds the active site non-covalently, resembling the substrate, and can be displaced by raising the substrate concentration; a compound forming a strong (covalent) bond with the enzyme is by definition not competing reversibly for the site.
explanations.B: Correct. Irreversible inhibition permanently disables an enzyme, unlike competitive or allosteric inhibition, which are reversible. It works either by blocking a required cofactor or, as in this case, by chemically modifying part of the apoenzyme itself — heavy-metal ions and organophosphate-type compounds are classic examples that combine covalently and essentially permanently with a catalytically important group on the enzyme, which is exactly the 'strong bond' the question describes for acetylcholinesterase.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Reversible non-competitive (allosteric) inhibitors bind a site other than the active site and can dissociate, restoring enzyme activity; this is the opposite of the strong, essentially permanent binding described in the question.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Negative feedback inhibition describes a pathway's own end product reversibly slowing an earlier enzyme in that same pathway to regulate flux, which is unrelated to an external toxic compound covalently disabling an unrelated enzyme like acetylcholinesterase.

questions.learning_objective: Classify a toxic compound that permanently disables an enzyme by covalent bonding as an irreversible inhibitor.

questions.title: Primary component of the cell membrane
questions.subject: fnd
questions.source_citation: Formative and Past Exams 2021 Q30 (also 2022 Q10)
questions.question: Which of the following correctly lists the primary biochemical components forming the cell membrane?

options.B: Only simple triglycerides and structural proteins
options.C: Cholesterol molecules and large nucleic acids

explanations.A: Correct. The cell membrane is built as a phospholipid bilayer with cholesterol interspersed between the phospholipid molecules, and with peripheral and integral proteins embedded in or attached to that bilayer, plus carbohydrate chains on its outer face. Phospholipids are named as the primary component because they form the continuous bilayer scaffold — with a hydrophilic head facing the aqueous environments on each side and a hydrophobic tail buried in the middle — into which every other membrane component is set, which is the fluid mosaic model.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Triglycerides are storage fats built for energy storage in adipocytes, not membrane-forming lipids; they lack the polar head group phospholipids have, so they cannot assemble into a stable bilayer the way phospholipids do.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Cholesterol is genuinely a membrane component, sitting among the phospholipids to modulate membrane fluidity, but nucleic acids play no structural role in the membrane at all — DNA and RNA are confined to the nucleus and cytoplasm, not built into the lipid bilayer.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Membrane proteins are important functional components — channels, receptors, transporters — but they are embedded within or attached to the phospholipid bilayer rather than forming the membrane by themselves; a membrane made 'exclusively' of protein channels would have no continuous barrier to hold them in place.

questions.subtopic: Cell membrane structure — fluid mosaic model
questions.learning_objective: Name phospholipids as the bilayer-forming component of the cell membrane, alongside cholesterol, membrane proteins and surface carbohydrate.

questions.title: Base classification of the nitrogenous base in GTP
questions.subject: fnd
questions.module_subject: SCU-FBS102 > Biochemistry > Nucleic Acids > Nucleotide Structure
questions.source_citation: Formative and Past Exams 2021 Q13 (also 2023 Q13)
questions.question: What is the specific chemical classification of the nitrogenous base found in a guanosine triphosphate molecule?

options.D: A very long complex fatty acid

explanations.A: Incorrect. Pyrimidines — cytosine, uracil and thymine — are the single-ring nitrogenous bases; guanine, the base named in guanosine triphosphate, is not one of them.
explanations.B: Correct. Nitrogenous bases split into two chemical classes: purines, which are adenine and guanine, and pyrimidines, which are cytosine, uracil and thymine. Guanosine triphosphate is built from the base guanine, so its base belongs to the purine class, distinguished structurally by its fused double-ring (a six-membered ring fused to a five-membered ring) rather than the single ring of a pyrimidine.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Nitrogenous bases are not amino acids; they are heterocyclic ring compounds that pair with a pentose sugar and phosphate to build a nucleotide, an entirely separate class of molecule from the amino acids that build proteins.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A fatty acid is a long hydrocarbon chain with a terminal carboxyl group, structurally unrelated to the ringed, nitrogen-containing base of a nucleotide.

questions.subtopic: Nucleotide structure — purine and pyrimidine bases
questions.learning_objective: Classify guanine, the base in GTP, as a purine, and distinguish the purine and pyrimidine base classes.

questions.title: Carbohydrate classified as a sugar alcohol
questions.subject: fnd
questions.source_citation: Formative and Past Exams 2021 Q58 (also 2022 Q38)
questions.question: Which of the following biochemical molecules is structurally classified as a carbohydrates alcohol or polyol?

options.A: The completely standard and highly basic glucose molecule
options.C: The five carbon containing active structural ribulose sugar
options.D: The very simple three carbon chain glyceraldehyde molecule

explanations.A: Incorrect. Glucose is an aldose monosaccharide with its carbonyl group intact; it is the parent sugar that can itself be reduced to a sugar alcohol (sorbitol), but glucose itself is not a sugar alcohol.
explanations.B: Correct. Monosaccharides are chemically modified into several classes of derivative, and sugar alcohols (polyols) form when a monosaccharide's carbonyl group is reduced to a hydroxyl group instead. Ribitol is exactly this — the sugar alcohol of the five-carbon sugar ribose — and it is best known as a structural component of riboflavin (vitamin B2), which is where FOMSCU's own biochemistry course meets it.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Ribulose is a five-carbon ketose sugar, an isomer related to ribose that still carries its carbonyl group intact; being reduced to ribitol is what would make it a sugar alcohol, but ribulose itself has not undergone that reduction.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Glyceraldehyde is a three-carbon aldose with its carbonyl group intact (an intermediate of glycolysis); its reduced sugar-alcohol form is glycerol, not glyceraldehyde itself.

questions.learning_objective: Identify ribitol as the sugar-alcohol derivative of ribose and a structural component of riboflavin.

questions.title: Protein level stabilised by side-chain R groups
questions.subject: fnd
questions.source_citation: EOY 2026 Q49
questions.question: The side chain R group plays an incredibly important role in stabilizing which specific protein level?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Primary structure is simply the linear sequence of amino acids linked by peptide bonds; it is defined by the backbone connectivity, not by any interaction of the side chains with one another.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Secondary structure — the alpha-helix and beta-pleated sheet — is held together by hydrogen bonds between backbone NH and C=O groups, which is a property of the peptide backbone itself rather than of the side chains.
explanations.C: Correct. Tertiary structure is the folding of a polypeptide chain into its specific three-dimensional globular shape, and it is maintained by several kinds of side-chain interaction: hydrophobic clustering of nonpolar R groups away from water, electrostatic (salt-bridge) bonds between oppositely charged R groups such as lysine and aspartate, hydrogen bonds involving side-chain hydroxyl, amide or carboxyl groups, and disulphide bonds between cysteine side chains. Because it is specifically the R group of each residue, not the shared backbone, that provides all of these stabilising interactions, tertiary structure is the level the R group is most responsible for.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Quaternary structure describes how separate polypeptide subunits associate into a multi-chain protein complex; the same kinds of side-chain interaction help hold subunits together, but the R group's defining, best-known role is folding a single chain into its tertiary structure first.

questions.learning_objective: Identify tertiary structure as the protein level stabilised by side-chain (R group) interactions such as hydrophobic clustering, salt bridges and disulphide bonds.

questions.title: Characteristic bond of protein secondary structure
questions.subject: fnd
questions.source_citation: EOM 2026 Q4
questions.question: Which bond is the characteristic bond responsible for stabilizing the secondary protein structure?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Hydrophobic interactions between nonpolar side chains help drive and stabilise tertiary folding, clustering nonpolar residues away from water, but they are not what holds the backbone in its regular secondary-structure coil or sheet.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The covalent peptide bond links successive amino acids into the chain (defining primary structure), and the covalent disulphide bond can cross-link cysteines in tertiary or quaternary structure; neither is the bond that produces the regular helical or sheet-like secondary folding pattern.
explanations.C: Correct. Secondary structure is mainly the alpha-helix or the beta-pleated sheet, and both are held together by hydrogen bonds between backbone atoms — in the alpha-helix, between the NH group of one peptide bond and the C=O group of a peptide bond further along the same chain, coiling it into a specific, repeating shape. This backbone hydrogen bonding is the characteristic, defining stabilising force of secondary structure, distinguishing it from the side-chain interactions that stabilise tertiary structure.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Ionic (electrostatic) bonds between charged side chains, such as a salt bridge between lysine and aspartate, contribute to tertiary structure rather than to the backbone folding of secondary structure.

questions.learning_objective: State that hydrogen bonds between backbone atoms hold together the alpha-helix and beta-pleated sheet of secondary structure.

questions.title: Process occurring during S phase
questions.subject: fnd
questions.source_citation: EOY 2026 Q39
questions.question: Which of the following critical processes occurs specifically during the S phase of the cell cycle?

explanations.A: Incorrect. General cell growth, along with the synthesis of RNA and proteins needed for eventual DNA replication, is the hallmark of the G1 (first gap) phase, which comes before S phase, not the defining event of S phase itself.
explanations.B: Correct. DNA replication is the process by which a double-stranded DNA molecule is copied into two identical daughter molecules, and it is confined to the synthesis (S) phase of interphase. Each parental strand acts as a template for a new complementary strand, so the mechanism is semi-conservative — every resulting daughter DNA molecule carries one old strand and one newly made strand — and it is this S-phase replication that doubles the cell's DNA content before mitosis.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Spindle formation happens during prophase and prometaphase of mitosis (M phase), well after S phase has already doubled the DNA content.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Cytokinesis is the physical division of the cytoplasm into two daughter cells, occurring at the very end of M phase, long after the S-phase replication that this question asks about.

questions.learning_objective: State that DNA replication, a semi-conservative process, is confined to the S phase of the cell cycle.

questions.title: Germ layer origin of the trilaminar disc
questions.subject: dev
questions.source_citation: Formative and Past Exams 2021 Q33 (also 2022 Q13)
questions.question: From which specific embryonic germ layer does the trilaminar disc ultimately derive during early development?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The hypoblast is one of the two layers of the earlier bilaminar disc, and it is the layer that epiblast cells invaginate through and replace during gastrulation, not the layer that gives rise to all three definitive germ layers.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The trophoblast is the outer layer of the blastocyst that goes on to form the placenta and fetal membranes; it is not part of the embryonic disc and does not contribute to the trilaminar disc's own three germ layers.
explanations.C: Correct. Gastrulation transforms the bilaminar embryonic disc into a trilaminar one during the third gestational week. It begins with formation of the primitive streak in the epiblast, and epiblast cells then invaginate through the primitive groove: some replace the hypoblast to form the endoderm, some remain to form the ectoderm, and others migrate between the two to form the intraembryonic mesoderm — so all three definitive germ layers of the trilaminar disc are epiblast-derived.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Extraembryonic mesoderm supports the developing placenta and membranes outside the embryo proper; the trilaminar disc's own three layers are intraembryonic and epiblast-derived, a separate lineage from the extraembryonic tissue.

questions.learning_objective: State that all three germ layers of the trilaminar disc — ectoderm, mesoderm and endoderm — are derived from the epiblast during gastrulation.

questions.title: Stage when chromosomal DNA replicates
questions.subject: fnd
questions.source_citation: Formative and Past Exams 2021 Q40 (also 2022 Q20)
questions.question: At which specific stage of mitosis does the process of chromosomal DNA replication actually occur?

options.A: During the highly active prophase stage
options.B: In the middle of the metaphase stage
options.D: During the final dividing telophase stage

explanations.A: Incorrect. Prophase is a stage of mitosis itself, when chromosomes condense and become visible by light microscopy; by this stage the DNA has already been fully replicated during the preceding interphase.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Metaphase is when the already-duplicated, condensed chromosomes align at the equatorial plate before separation — again well after replication is complete, not the stage when it happens.
explanations.C: Correct. The cell cycle divides into mitosis (the period of visible division) and interphase (the period between two successive divisions, itself split into G1, S and G2 sub-phases). Chromosomal DNA replication is confined to the S (synthesis) sub-phase of interphase — before the cell ever enters visible mitotic division — so despite the question's phrasing, the replication it describes belongs to interphase, not to any stage within mitosis itself.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Telophase is the final stage of mitosis, when the two sets of already-separated chromosomes decondense inside two new nuclei; DNA replication is long finished by this point, from the preceding interphase.

questions.learning_objective: State that chromosomal DNA replication occurs during interphase (specifically its S sub-phase), before the cell enters mitosis.

questions.title: Checkpoint controlling entry into mitosis
questions.subject: fnd
questions.source_citation: Formative and Past Exams 2021 Q52 (also 2022 Q32)
questions.question: At which of the following specific cell cycle checkpoints is the process of mitosis officially controlled and permitted to proceed?

options.A: The very first initial growth G1 phase
options.B: The second later growth G2 phase checkpoint
options.D: The highly active DNA synthesis S phase

explanations.A: Incorrect. The G1 checkpoint verifies cell size, nutrients, growth factors and DNA integrity before the cell commits to replicating its DNA at all; it gates entry into S phase, not entry into mitosis itself.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The G2 checkpoint checks cell size and DNA integrity after replication is complete, before the cell is allowed to enter mitosis — an important checkpoint, but not the one that controls mitosis while it is under way.
explanations.C: Correct. Three checkpoints police the cell cycle: G1 (before DNA replication), G2 (before mitosis begins) and the spindle-assembly checkpoint, which operates within M phase itself. The spindle-assembly checkpoint checks that every chromosome is properly attached to the mitotic spindle before allowing anaphase to start, which is the specific point at which mitosis's own progression is directly controlled and permitted to proceed.
explanations.D: Incorrect. S phase is when DNA replication itself occurs, governed by the G1 checkpoint that precedes it; it has no checkpoint of its own that controls mitosis, which happens afterwards in M phase.

questions.learning_objective: Name the spindle-assembly checkpoint within M phase as the checkpoint that controls progression through mitosis itself.

questions.title: Cell-cycle phase of genomic DNA replication
questions.subject: fnd
questions.source_citation: Formative and Past Exams 2021 Q15 (also 2023 Q15)
questions.question: During which specific phase of the eukaryotic cell cycle does the replication of genomic DNA occur?

options.A: The first initial gap growth phase
options.C: The second later gap growth phase
options.D: The active mitotic nuclear division phase

explanations.A: Incorrect. G1, the first gap phase, is when the cell grows, acquires energy and synthesises the RNA and proteins needed for the coming replication — it prepares for DNA synthesis but is not the phase in which replication itself occurs.
explanations.B: Correct. Interphase is subdivided into three phases — G1, S and G2 — and it is specifically the S (synthesis) phase in which the cell's entire genomic DNA content is replicated, doubling each chromosome into two identical sister chromatids joined at a centromere. This replicated DNA is what mitosis will later distribute equally into two daughter cells.
explanations.C: Incorrect. G2, the second gap phase, comes after DNA replication is already finished; the cell uses it to check for replication errors and prepare for mitosis, not to replicate DNA.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Mitosis is the visible division of the already-doubled genetic material into two nuclei; by the time the cell enters mitosis, DNA replication (from S phase) is long complete.

questions.learning_objective: Name the S (synthesis) phase of interphase as when the cell's genomic DNA is replicated.

questions.title: EM appearance of thick myosin filaments
questions.subject: msk
questions.source_citation: Formative and Past Exams 2021 Q16 (also 2023 Q16)
questions.question: How do the thick myosin filaments primarily appear when observed in a striated muscle under an electron microscope?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The isotropic (I) band is the light band flanking each side of the Z line; it is built only of thin actin filaments where they do not overlap with myosin, which is why it appears light rather than dark.
explanations.B: Correct. The sarcomere, the segment between two adjacent Z lines, is the basic contractile unit of striated muscle. Within it, the thick myosin filaments are restricted to a central region called the anisotropic (A) band, and because thick filaments are dense and, where they overlap thin filaments, doubly dense, this region appears as the dark band of the classic light-and-dark banding pattern seen under both light and electron microscopy.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The H zone is the paler central region of the A band where thick filaments are present but not overlapped by thin filaments; it is lighter than the rest of the A band, not the answer describing the myosin filaments' overall appearance.
explanations.D: Incorrect. There is no bright or luminescent band in the sarcomere's structure; ordinary electron microscopy shows density contrast (dark versus light), not luminescence, and the myosin-containing region is the dense, dark one.

questions.subtopic: Sarcomere structure — A and I bands
questions.learning_objective: State that the thick myosin filaments occupy the dark A band of the sarcomere.

questions.title: Organelle that modifies and packages proteins
questions.subject: fnd
questions.source_citation: EOM 2026 Q10
questions.question: Which specific cellular organelle is primarily responsible for modifying and packaging proteins?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Smooth endoplasmic reticulum has no ribosomes and specialises in lipid synthesis, steroid hormone production and detoxification, rather than modifying or packaging protein.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Rough endoplasmic reticulum, studded with ribosomes, is where secreted and membrane proteins are first synthesised and undergo initial folding — it hands its product forward to the Golgi for the modification and packaging step, rather than performing that step itself.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Lysosomes are single-membrane bags of hydrolytic digestive enzymes, themselves one of the Golgi's own downstream products, not the organelle that does the modifying and packaging.
explanations.D: Correct. On electron microscopy the Golgi apparatus is a stack of three to ten flat, curved saccules: its entry (cis) face receives transfer vesicles from the rough endoplasmic reticulum, and its exit (trans) face buds off finished products. In between, the Golgi packs and concentrates protein, chemically modifies it by adding carbohydrate to make glycoproteins, and forms the secretory vesicles and primary lysosomes that leave the cell or its cytoplasm — which is exactly the modifying-and-packaging role the question describes.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the Golgi apparatus as the organelle that modifies and packages protein arriving from the rough endoplasmic reticulum.

questions.title: Organelle responsible for packaging protein
questions.subject: fnd
questions.source_citation: EOY 2026 Q23
questions.question: Which cellular organelle is primarily responsible for the packaging of protein?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Mitochondria generate ATP through oxidative phosphorylation and have no role in modifying or packaging secretory protein.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Smooth endoplasmic reticulum lacks ribosomes and specialises in lipid and steroid synthesis and detoxification reactions, not in handling protein produced elsewhere in the cell.
explanations.C: Correct. On electron microscopy the Golgi complex is a stack of parallel flat saccules with a cis (entry) face receiving transfer vesicles from the rough endoplasmic reticulum and a trans (exit) face budding off finished products. The Golgi packs, concentrates and chemically modifies incoming protein — adding carbohydrate to build glycoproteins — before forming the secretory vesicles, primary lysosomes and coated vesicles that carry the finished, packaged product on to its destination.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Lysosomes are themselves one of the packaged products the Golgi forms and buds off from its trans face; they digest material with their hydrolytic enzymes rather than doing the packaging.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the Golgi complex as the organelle responsible for packaging protein for secretion.

field_notes.fomscu: EOY 2026 Q23; source-JSON extraction, bank tier. Shares CON-FND-405BB5EA3C359E with histology-golgi-apparatus.

questions.title: Site of ribosomal RNA synthesis
questions.subject: fnd
questions.source_citation: EOM 2026 Q2
questions.question: Where is ribosomal RNA synthesized within the cell?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Smooth endoplasmic reticulum handles lipid synthesis and detoxification, not the transcription of ribosomal genes, which requires the ribosomal DNA held in the nucleus.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Lysosomes digest material with hydrolytic enzymes; they have no role in RNA synthesis of any kind.
explanations.C: Correct. A ribosome is a non-membranous particle made of ribosomal RNA and protein. Its rRNA is transcribed inside the nucleolus, from the clustered ribosomal genes located there, while the proteins that will join it are made separately in the cytoplasm and imported back into the nucleolus; the rRNA and protein then unite there into the large and small ribosomal subunits, which are exported separately to the cytoplasm and only join together, around a strand of messenger RNA, during protein synthesis.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The Golgi apparatus modifies and packages protein that has already been made; it plays no part in the synthesis of RNA.

questions.learning_objective: State that ribosomal RNA is transcribed in the nucleolus, where it unites with imported ribosomal protein to form the ribosomal subunits.

questions.title: Most common neuron shape — motor neurons
questions.subject: fnd
questions.source_citation: Formative and Past Exams 2021 Q37 (also 2022 Q17)
questions.question: What is structurally considered the most common morphological shape of a typical motor neuron in the human body?

options.A: The simple bipolar sensory neuron shape
options.D: The very rare unipolar round shape

explanations.A: Incorrect. True bipolar neurons, with two separate processes at opposite poles of the cell body, are a rare, specialised sensory shape found in the retina and vestibulocochlear ganglia, not the shape of a typical motor neuron.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Pseudounipolar neurons are the sensory cells of the dorsal root and cranial sensory ganglia, whose two embryonic processes fuse into a single stalk near the soma; this is a sensory pattern, not a motor one.
explanations.C: Correct. Nerve cells are classed by how many processes leave the cell body — one, two, or more than two. Multipolar neurons, with many dendrites and a single axon, are by far the most numerous shape in the human nervous system, and this is specifically the shape of motor neurons, such as the large multipolar cells in the anterior horn of the spinal cord that innervate skeletal muscle.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A truly unipolar cell, with a single process arising directly from the soma and no history of fusion from two earlier processes, is essentially absent in humans; it is not a shape found among ordinary motor neurons.

questions.subtopic: Classification of neurons by process number
questions.learning_objective: Identify the multipolar shape, with many dendrites and one axon, as the most common neuron morphology and the shape of a typical motor neuron.

questions.title: Connective tissue layer around one nerve fascicle
questions.subject: neuro
questions.module_subject: SCU-FBS102 > Histology > Nervous Tissue > Peripheral Nerve Coverings
questions.source_citation: Formative and Past Exams 2021 Q46 (also 2022 Q26)
questions.question: In a normal peripheral nerve trunk what is the specific connective tissue layer that closely surrounds a single nerve bundle?

options.A: The extremely delicate inner endoneurium layer
options.C: The massively thick outer epineurium layer
options.D: The entirely distinct muscular outer epimysium

explanations.A: Incorrect. The endoneurium is the finest of the three coverings, a delicate layer of connective tissue that surrounds each individual nerve fibre within a fascicle, one level deeper than the covering around the whole fascicle that this question asks about.
explanations.B: Correct. A peripheral nerve trunk is wrapped, from outside in, by three layers: the epineurium around the whole trunk, the perineurium around each individual fascicle (bundle of nerve fibres), and the endoneurium around each single nerve fibre within a fascicle. The perineurium is built of layered flattened cells joined by tight junctions, which makes it the layer that forms the blood-nerve barrier around each fascicle — exactly the 'single nerve bundle' covering the question describes.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The epineurium is the outermost, densest connective-tissue sheath, wrapping the whole nerve trunk (all of its fascicles together), not a single fascicle on its own.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Epimysium is the connective-tissue covering of a whole skeletal muscle, an entirely different tissue system from the coverings of a peripheral nerve, and it plays no part in wrapping nerve fascicles.

questions.learning_objective: Name the perineurium as the connective-tissue layer, forming the blood-nerve barrier, that surrounds each individual nerve fascicle.

questions.title: Epithelium of the epidermis
questions.subject: fnd
questions.module_subject: SCU-FBS102 > Histology > General Histology > Epithelial Tissue
questions.source_citation: EOY 2026 Q27
questions.question: Which specific type of epithelial tissue exists in the epidermis of the skin?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Simple squamous epithelium is a single layer of flat cells, suited to sites needing rapid diffusion such as capillary walls and alveoli; it has none of the many stacked, protective layers the epidermis needs against abrasion and water loss.
explanations.B: Correct. Both keratinized and non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium are many layers of polyhedral cells with rounded central nuclei, becoming progressively flatter towards the surface, resting on a basement membrane over connective tissue. In the keratinized form the surface cells are replaced by an acidophilic, anuclear horny layer of condensed keratin, and this is the type that covers the epidermis of the skin, protecting it against abrasion, friction and water loss in a way a non-keratinized wet lining, such as the oral mucosa, does not.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Stratified cuboidal epithelium, with two or more layers of roughly cube-shaped cells, lines structures such as sweat gland ducts, not the multilayered, flattening, keratin-forming epithelium of the skin.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Pseudostratified columnar epithelium looks layered because nuclei sit at different heights but every cell touches the basement membrane; it lines much of the respiratory tract, an entirely different structure and function from the true multilayered, keratinizing epidermis.

questions.learning_objective: Identify keratinized stratified squamous epithelium as the tissue covering the epidermis, and distinguish it from the non-keratinized form.

questions.title: Elastic connective tissue of large arteries
questions.subject: fnd
questions.module_subject: SCU-FBS102 > Histology > Connective Tissue > Types of Connective Tissue Proper
questions.source_citation: EOY 2026 Q36
questions.question: Which type of connective tissue has elasticity and exists in large arteries like the aorta?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Reticular connective tissue is a fine meshwork of type III collagen fibres that forms the supporting stroma of organs such as the liver, spleen and lymph nodes; it provides a structural scaffold rather than the elastic recoil needed by a large artery wall.
explanations.B: Incorrect. White fibrous connective tissue is dense, mainly type I collagen, built for tensile strength in structures such as tendons and ligaments — strong but not markedly elastic, the opposite property from what a large artery's wall needs.
explanations.C: Correct. Yellow elastic connective tissue is a dense field of thin, single, zigzagging elastic fibres, yellow in the fresh state because of their elastin content. Its defining property is elastic recoil, which is exactly why it is found in the walls of large (elastic) arteries such as the aorta, letting the vessel stretch during systole and spring back during diastole to keep blood flowing onward.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Mucoid connective tissue is the soft, gelatinous tissue of the umbilical cord (Wharton's jelly), built for cushioning rather than elastic recoil, and it is not the tissue found in the wall of a large artery.

questions.learning_objective: Identify yellow elastic connective tissue as the tissue giving large (elastic) arteries such as the aorta their recoil.

questions.title: Nuclear molecule that associates with protein
questions.subject: fnd
questions.source_citation: Formative and Past Exams 2021 Q77 (also 2022 Q56)
questions.question: Which of the following molecules is specifically made inside the nucleus of a cell and associates with proteins to form ribosomes?

options.A: The highly active completely entirely functional long messenger mRNA
options.C: The extremely busy completely transporting strictly specific transfer tRNA
options.D: The highly specific entirely completely regulatory very short micro miRNA

explanations.A: Incorrect. Messenger RNA is transcribed in the nucleoplasm from protein-coding genes and then threads between ribosomal subunits to be translated; it does not itself combine with protein to build the ribosome's own structure.
explanations.B: Correct. A ribosome is a non-membranous particle formed of ribosomal RNA and protein. The rRNA component is transcribed specifically inside the nucleolus, where it then unites with ribosomal protein, imported from the cytoplasm, to assemble the large and small ribosomal subunits — this rRNA-protein association inside the nucleolus is exactly the process the question describes.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Transfer RNA carries amino acids to the ribosome during translation and pairs with mRNA codons via its anticodon; it is not a structural building block of the ribosome itself.
explanations.D: Incorrect. microRNA regulates gene expression by base-pairing with target mRNAs to block translation or promote their degradation; it plays no role in building the ribosome's rRNA-protein structure.

questions.learning_objective: Identify rRNA as the nucleolus-made RNA that unites with protein to form the ribosome.

questions.title: Transport mechanism for lipoprotein uptake
questions.subject: fnd
questions.module_subject: SCU-FBS102 > Physiology > Cell Physiology > Membrane Transport
questions.source_citation: EOY 2026 Q57
questions.question: Lipoproteins typically enter the target cells through which of the following cellular transport mechanisms?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Passive (simple) diffusion moves small, lipid-soluble molecules directly across the membrane down their concentration gradient; a large lipoprotein particle is far too big to cross the membrane this way.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Facilitated diffusion carries specific small solutes such as glucose through a dedicated carrier protein, still moving down a concentration gradient — a mechanism built for small solutes, not for taking in a large particle like a lipoprotein.
explanations.C: Correct. Endocytosis is the bulk movement of material into the cell by forming vesicles from the plasma membrane, and one of its three forms — receptor-mediated endocytosis — begins when a ligand binds its specific receptors on the cell surface; the receptors then cluster in a clathrin-coated patch of membrane that pinches off as a coated vesicle carrying the ligand inside. This is exactly the route lipoproteins such as LDL take, binding their receptor before being internalised whole, rather than crossing the membrane molecule by molecule.
explanations.D: Incorrect. 'Active diffusion' does not name a real transport mechanism; primary active transport moves solutes against their gradient using ATP directly, which is a different process from the vesicle-forming uptake that brings a whole lipoprotein particle into the cell.

questions.learning_objective: Identify receptor-mediated endocytosis as the mechanism by which lipoproteins are taken up whole into target cells.
